The first organized school in Kansas was organized in Wyandotte City by J.M. Armstrong in 1844.  It lasted until his death in 1852. The school had the distinction of being the first  established for white children in what is now the state of Kansas.  A school for whites was established in Council Grove in 1851 by Mr. T.S. Huffaker. The State of Kansas is challenged to find a county surpassing Jackson in its zealous devotion to educational matters.

Shortly after the county was organized in 1857, the people began to think about schools for their children.  The first school was taught in this county by Miss Hariet Warfield of Clay County Missouri in 1857. It was gotten up on the subscription plan, and held in a little log cabin, 10 feet square, located on the SW 1/4 section 23, township 9, range 16. This would put it about 5 miles east of Hoyt. (1) School was started in Jefferson township the same year. Mrs. H. S. Hart held school in her log cabin.

Hard times, drought, the coming of the Civil War and the internal strife in Kangas kept the people of Jackson County from doing much about schools until after 1861. (1) The first real school was built in the county in 1858. It was built out of logs and was also used as a church. Information from the Kansas State Historical Society, says that the lighting came from leaving out one log in the wall on one side. It was heated.  by a fireplace. It was taught by Miss Anna Parrot. The name of it was called Brick, and was also the first organized district in county. Permission for this was granted on June 20, 1859. It was located on land which was part of the Pottawatomie Reserve.
The school term was six months, three months in spring and three in the fall.
In 1868, George and Mary Hafer donated one acre of land to the school.
It was about 1/2 mile west of the log cabin. In the same year, Brick school was built. In one porch was W.H. Webster. He taught for seven terms. At one time there were 58 students.

The building was also used as a church until a church building was completed in 1890. In 1916 the second building was torn down and a building with a basement was erected. School was held here until it was destroyed by a tornado in 1962. The last teacher was Katherin Linehan. (The information about Brick was Kansas Historical Society and Forest Morris family and the Everette Gibson family.) The first school in Douglas township was built in 1859. It was a

log structure, 18x20 constructed by neighbors who worked together and did an agreed part of the work. Later "Star" was built. A group of people met Nov. 5, 1859 to organize district #12. They chose the site in March 17, 1860. This located in the SE corner SW 1/4 of section 22, township 9, range 16. Bainbridge Richards and Rippitoe were names frequently mentioned.
The first school in Jefferson was taught by Mrs. H.S. Hart. Ed Hulan taught the first one in Grant township in 1858 and the first building was built 1859.
Sophia Lattimer taught the first one in Liberty township in a log house on the subscription plan. James B. Hastings was the first teacher in Straight Creek and the first building was erected in 1859.
The first school in Tippinville was taught by Miss Rioce in the winter of 1857 and 1858 in her home. One source says the building was bout 1/4 mile east of the crossroads.

Alan Gardnier states the first building made of logs, was built where the cemetery south of Denison is. A few years later a school house was built on the Claud Braum shop lots where Denison now stands.

A log building housed the first one in Cedar township.  It was built by individual subecription on S.J. Elliot's land in 1858. It later moved 1 mile south. The next was built in 1862. (from Plate Book 1881 Cedar township.) There were at least 14 school districts formed in 1859. They were Brick, Holton, Denison, Center, Stone, (it was called Banner later) Liberty, Philo, Pleasant Valley, Lawn Ridge, Mulinax, Cenar Hill, North Star, Point Pleasant, Cedar Vale.

The first school in Holton was established in 1858 with the construction of a frame building at 415 Wisconsin Avenue. Only the lower grades were maintained at that time and continued in the original building until Central School was completed in 1875 at the corner of 5th and New Jersey.

Prof. C.Y. Roop organized the 1st high school in 1880 and the 1st graduation was in 1881. After establishment of high school classes, Central School was used as both grade and high school. The lower grades were conducted on the ground floor rooms and the high school on the upper floor.
Prof. Roop served as both superintendent and only teacher for the 3 students in the 1st high school class.

Colorado school was built in 1885 at the corner of 5th and Colorado Ave. Although this school had no direct relation to the high school, it was an integral part of the Holton school system which eventually produced high school students.
The first high school was built in 1906.  Campbell College at the north edge of Holton, was acquired for use as a larger high school in 1916.

At first the county was called Galhoun. On September 24, 1855 Jackson County was organized. This area went to the Kansas River. In 1868 the county was divided into two counties. We do not find any mention of a superintendent until 1859. He was Ira Taber. His name is signed to the first 14 districts.

In 1860, Jackson County had a population of 2,297 of which 396 were of school age 5 to to years oId. In 1872 this had increased to 2,587 and by 1880 to 3,855. In 1872 there were 51 districts and 6 joint districts, and by 18_2, this had increases to 70 with 6 joint districts. The population was greatest around Holton. Other than that more sundents were in the south part of the county.

DENISON SCHOOL from Alan Gardiners book The first school house, which was made of logs, was built where the cemetary south of town is now located. A few years later a stone school house was built on the Claud Braum shop lots where Denison now stands (1935). Later the school was moved to a half mile east of north cedar (Tippinville). Some of the early teachers were J. Gardiner, Mary Buckley-Buffon, Fanny Winter, Ellan Hux, assisted by her twin sister, Helen Hux, James Boyd, Mr. Gillett, Mr. Nuff Booth, David, Jane Gilleece, Mary Miligen, Richard (Dick) McClarren.

The pump to the well of the school house east of Tippenville, (unless recently removed) can still be seen on the south side ot the road a little more than a quarter mile east of the crossroads, Rev. Geo. Gardiner, the writer's grandfather, attended school at this place, attaining, perhaps the equivalent of a fifth grade education, which was not uncommon for those times.

The pioneer schools were held in rudely constructed log houses and provided with homemade furniture, the seats being made of puncheon, with wooden pegs for legs, and wooden pegs were driven into the wall to support a board which served as a desk for the pupils to rite upon.

Apparently the school house was moved into Denison in the summer of 1890. The moving of the school house from the old site to the present site in Denison left a debt of considerable proportion on the district and in consequence of this debt was quite a heavy tax for that year of 18 mills.
In 1909 a new block building was built across the street from the Methodist Church.
It was a 4-room, two story building, which held two grades each. As time went by the number of students out grew the building and one grade was moved into the high school.

The old Fairview school was moved in just north of the building. It held one class. It has since been torn down. A mobile building was moved across and up the street from the grade school and it held one grade. Since the closing of the high school, in 1969, the grade school has occupied the high school building.

During the winter of 1972-73 the old Denison school was demolished. The old bell from the grade school was donated to the Denison Alumni. Some of the blocks from the old building were used to make a base and the old bell was mounted on it as a memorial.
In 1883, there were 93 people from age 5-21 of which 88 attended part of the year with an average of 55 1/2. This decreased 1884 to 84 and 47 average.
Phebe A. Bradly was a teacher in 1871.

(Excerpt from 1898 and 99 anned Catalog) The people of Jackson desiring to establish an institution of higher learning met to discuss way and means. The result was a committee was formed to correspond with the Hon. A. G. Campbell, a wealthy miner who formery lived in Jackson County. The community raised $10,000 which Mr. Campbell matched plus $1100 to buy 11 acres of land north of 9th street, west of New York and east to Wisconsin. In 1880 a fine stone bulding 40x60, two stories and basement was created.
School opened in 1882 with 40 students, By By1887 it was necessary to enlarge the building. A building 50x100 with a basement was erected at this time. By 1890 a 2nd story was completed.

The 3 story building was constructed of native white limestone on artistic lines with painted spires and arched windows was regarded as the most beautiful building in northeast Kansas (Ruth A. Shackler) The college reached an enrollement of nearly 400, brick dormitories were built on the land south of 9th street.  The dormitory was enlarged to 50 rooms. The dining hall was enlarged to seat 75, it had steam heat and electric lights. (Rochelle Arnold) In 1889 the Bureau of Education in Washington classed Camplell Unversity with colleges and universities in the country. Campbell University was the only independent school on its list.

The cost of maintaining the University was more than the peple of Holton could handle. In 1913, the University merged with Lane University and the name called Campbell College and was operated by the United Brethren Church.  In 1912 the college merged again with the Kansas City University and things were moved to Kansas City.
The Holton facility was used as a junior college but the students had trouble getting their credits transferred to 4 yr schools. The buildings were torn down in 1930.
First Campbell College now the Lutheran church (1986).

Banner #5 in 1859. The original district included 15 sections but as time went on, this was changed several times. At first land in Jefferson and Franklin and Banner was included. Later some was detached to Maple Grove, Sunflower, Pleasant Valley and Winding Vale.
In 1883 there were 85 different students attending with 136 days taught and an average attendance of 46. This decreased in 1884 to 65 with an average of 31. The students ranged from 5 years to 20.
In 1884 they taught 173 days and had 86 students enrolled with an average attendance of 25. In ‘85 (1885) there were 62 students from 5 to 21 years.

Lawn Ridge was organized in 1859.  It included land in Liberty, Netawaka, Whiting and Straight Creek townships. Later, some land was detached to form Aurora.
In 1883 there were 50 students with an average of 24. They had 5 months of school.  In 85 there were only 44 students. Aurora was formed in ‘83 so this may indicate the reason for decline.

Cedar Hill was five miles south of Soldier. It was in the W ½  of NW 1/4 of section 10 in Grant township. It is still standing (3-86).

North Star #12 was organized Nov 5, 1859. According to the minutes of the organization meeting, the meeting was held in the Point Pleasant school.  The minutes up to March 28, 1872 call it point Pleasant. After then, they read Star.  It was located on the SE corner SW1/4 - 22 - 9 south. Alpheus Bainbridge, chairman; Alfred Richards, clerk.
A new building was built in 1886. Due to population increase, the district split and South Star was built (dist 76).  In 1885 there were 84 pupils in Star.
The records show Point Pleasant was organized in 1859.  This was apparently Star #12.  Due to increase in population the district split.

The record attendance was 55 in 1885. The teacher was Maggie Robson. The salary was $40.

Mrs Alice Wamego gave the bottom picture and some interesting facts. She went to this school en 1906.  Her father, Thomas Marshall, Harry Tutt, and John Summers were on the board for years. There was no well so the pupils carried the water in a bucket from Harry Tutts. Her father came home from a board meting very disturbed, because the teacher they wanted was asking $50 a month. She was a good one, She cleaned the building and kept the fire going.  Many pupils were older than she.

During the years of 1908 through 1918, the students attended a two-story frame school which was located on the northeast side of Hoyt. It was a two-year high school from 1908-1911. From 1912-1917, the term was increased to three years. The school year consisted of nine months Due to change in the requirements, there were no graduates this year as they returned the next year for their fourth year In 1918, there were 39 pupil and 3 teachers The school was classified as a class D school The graduation exercises were held April 1? on a Friday evening at the ME Church and the speaker was Gov Capper. On May 23, 1918, school closed with a picnic at Woburn school with Professor Reid and Miss Weightman in
attendance.  We transferred to the new building on New Years Day, January 1, 1919.
